qtr.text: Nothing, or almost nothing, can be said about accent - much less about tone - in Quepo, since, first, no word of this language has survived; second, the materials available for this study do not allow accentual positions to be identified, owing to the scarcity of data. In some cases vowel alternations appear in final position, which suggests that, at least, the final vowel did not carry the main accent: Beara ~ Beare, Oco ~ Ocu. In these cases it would seem that Quepo had paroxytone (penult-stressed) words.

5292.dq: Inference from spelling variation of anthroponyms in colonial manuscripts, not from spoken data; no words of the language survive; the statement is explicitly an admission of undeterminability with a speculative paroxytone hint.
5292.prule: Author states accent position (and a fortiori tone) cannot be determined from the surviving material (16th-17th c. Spanish transcriptions of proper names); the only hint is that final-vowel spelling alternations (Beara~Beare, Oco~Ocu) suggest the final vowel was unstressed, i.e. possibly penultimate stress in those names; Areba~Arebe~Aribe, if one name, would be antepenultimate.
5292.quote: Nada, o casi nada, se puede decir del acento -mucho menos del tono- en quepo, ya que, en primer lugar, no existe ninguna palabra en este idioma que haya sobrevivido; en segundo lugar, los materiales con que se cuenta para el presente estudio no permiten identificar posiciones acentuales, debido a la escasez de datos. En algunos casos se presentan alternancias vocálicas en posición final, lo cual da a entender que, al menos, la vocal final no llevaba el acento principal: Beara - Beare, Oco - Ocu. En estos casos, pareciera que el quepo tenía palabras graves.
5292.loc: p. 69, section 3.4 '¿Acento o tono en quepo?'
5292.idn: Quepo, the extinct language of the Quepos of the southern Pacific region of Costa Rica (provincia de Quepo), known only from anthroponyms in 16th-17th century Spanish manuscripts.
5292.exq_: Areba - Arebe - Aribe: if the same anthroponym, 'sería un caso de palabra esdrújula' (antepenult), since only initial <a> is invariant; author flags no certainty it is one name.

evidence_works.detail: A 110-item Yinbaw Swadesh list (103 items attested) extracted from Ken Manson's unpublished Excel field database ('Manson Ms.'), printed with tone diacritics on every form. The Yinbaw section says only 'The transcription is essentially the same as for Pekon Kayan' (p. 8), and the Pekon Kayan section states '(c) a system of six tones is postulated, which can also be phonologically interpreted as four tones plus an additional parameter of breathiness' (p. 7). The tone-count statement is made for Pekon Kayan, not Yinbaw; Yinbaw inherits it only as a transcription convention. No stress or accent statement for Yinbaw anywhere.

evidence_works.detail: An annotated bibliography; the Yinbaw ('Yeinbaw') content is a second-hand summary of two unpublished 1992 manuscripts by J. Fraser Bennett. Under 'Interim findings report: Central Karen investigation' it prints a tone box for Padaung and Yeinbaw by proto-tone category (A, B, D) and proto-initial voicing: 'Yeinbaw A B D: non-vd 5 1 5, voiced 3̤ 1̤ 5̤' (p. 2), i.e. tone values with a breathy-register series on the proto-voiced column. Under 'Phonetics and phonology of Karen languages' it reports: 'Notes the retention of final [n, ŋ] in Padaung, but lost in Yeinbaw. Proto-voiced became voiceless with a register contrast (breathy phonation). Proto-stop final syllables remain distinct in both Yeinbaw and Padaung (no comment on Zayein or Gekhu).' (p. 2). No stress, accent or prominence remark anywhere in the 9 pages.

5315.prule: Primary stress falls on the word-initial syllable: a single quantity-insensitive trochee aligned at the left edge (OT: TROCHEE, ALL-FT-L); syllable weight plays no role. Established philologically from Henshaw's accent marks (214 stress-marked words, 73% initial).
